title: Packages and archives
goal: Pack and unpack releases with tar, gzip and zip, verify downloads with checksums, and find out where a command or package comes from.
setup: # P2/P6: files offered by a local "download server"
# P4: a text report to compress
for i in $(seq 1 200); do echo "2026-10-20 report line $i: all services OK"; done > report.txt

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Make a compressed backup of app/, save the checksum of the backup file,' '# then test a restore into restore-test/ and compare it with app/.' 'tar -cfz backup.tar.gz app' 'sha256sum app > backup.sha256' 'tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C restore-test' 'echo "backup OK"' > backup.sh

problems.title: tar: create, list and extract a release
problems.situation: The Jenkins pipeline must pack the to-do API into `todo-api-2.4.1.tar.gz`, check what is inside, and the server must unpack it into a release folder. The secret `.env` must not be in the archive.
task: Create `todo-api-2.4.1.tar.gz` from the folder `app` (`-czf`).
List the contents without extracting (`-tzf`). Sort the list.
Create it again without `.env` (use `--exclude`). List again.
Extract it into a new folder `releases/2.4.1` (`-xzf ... -C`). Show the result with `find`.
hints: c = create, x = extract, t = list, z = gzip, f = file name (must come last, right before the name).
`--exclude='.env'` goes before the folder name.
`-C DIR` = change to DIR first. The folder must exist: `mkdir -p` it.

explanation.meaning: Create a gzip-compressed archive of DIR.
List the files inside. Check before extracting on a server.
Leave matching files out.
Extract into DIR (it must exist).
bzip2 / xz compression instead of gzip (`.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz`). Modern tar also detects it when extracting.

mistakes: `tar -cfz backup.tar.gz app`: `f` takes the next word as the file name, so the archive is called `z` (P5).
Extracting a tar from the internet into `/` or the home folder without listing it first: it can overwrite files.
`tar -xzf file.tar.gz -C dir` when `dir` is missing: `tar: dir: Cannot open: No such file or directory`.

checks.run: tar -xzf todo.tgz -C missing-dir 2>&1; tar -czf t.tgz app; tar -xzf t.tgz -C missing-dir
checks.expect: tar: missing-dir: Cannot open: No such file or directory

problems.interview_say: I create archives with `tar -czf name.tar.gz dir`, check them with `tar -tzf`, and extract with `tar -xzf name.tar.gz -C target`. `f` always comes last, directly before the file name.
problems.try_yourself: Run `tar -czvf test.tgz app` (with `v`). Then `tar -tvzf test.tgz`. What extra information does `v` show?

problems.title: Download and verify with sha256sum
problems.situation: A Dockerfile downloads the `todo-cli` tool. If the file is changed on the way (broken mirror, attacker), the build must fail. The vendor publishes a SHA-256 checksum. Here a local test server plays the vendor's website.
task: Start a download server: `python3 -m http.server 8091 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory dist &`.
Download `todo-cli.sh` with `curl -fsSL -o`, and again with `wget -q -O`.
Download `todo-cli.sh.sha256` and check the file with `sha256sum -c`.
Change one byte of the downloaded file and check again. Print the exit code.
hints: `curl -fsSL -o FILE URL`: fail on errors, silent, follow redirects, save to FILE.
A `.sha256` file has lines `HASH  FILENAME`. `sha256sum -c` checks every line.
`sha256sum -c` exits 1 when a file does not match. Use that to stop a build.
solution: cmp todo-cli.sh todo-cli-wget.sh && echo "curl and wget got the same file"
echo "# changed" >> todo-cli.sh            # simulate a broken or changed download

explanation.meaning: Download to a file, fail on HTTP errors, follow redirects (`-L`).
The same with wget: quiet, output file.
Compare two files byte by byte; no output if they are equal.
Recompute the hash and compare with the expected one: `OK` or `FAILED`.
A mismatch. In a Dockerfile `RUN` or a CI step, this stops the build.

problems.expected_output:
curl and wget got the same file
todo-cli.sh: OK
todo-cli.sh: FAILED
sha256sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match
exit code: 1
mistakes: Downloading the checksum from the same untrusted place as the file. Get it from the vendor's official page or a signed release.
`curl URL | bash` installs without any check. Download, verify, then run.
problems.interview_say: I download with `curl -fsSL -o file URL`, then verify with `sha256sum -c` against the published checksum, so a changed or broken file stops the build.
problems.try_yourself: Compute a checksum yourself: `sha256sum app/start.sh`. Change the file and compute it again.

problems.title: apt and dpkg: what is installed, and from which package?
problems.situation: A script on the server uses `tree` and `ls`. The user must know which package each command comes from (to add them to a Dockerfile), and check if a package is installed. Installing needs sudo; these checks do not.
task: Find the package that owns `/usr/bin/ls` with `dpkg -S`.
Check if `coreutils` is installed with `dpkg -l` (first two columns).
List the files of the `tree` package that are in a `bin` folder (`dpkg -L`).
Show the installed and candidate version of `tree` with `apt-cache policy`.
Read the table: apt vs dnf/yum for the same tasks.
hints: `dpkg -S /path` = which package owns this file. `dpkg -L pkg` = files of a package.
In `dpkg -l`, `ii` = installed OK.
`apt-cache policy pkg` shows `Installed:` and `Candidate:`.

explanation.meaning: Search: which installed package owns this file.
Package status. `ii` = desired install, is installed.
All files that the package installed.
Installed version, candidate (newest available) version, and the repository.
Refresh the package lists. Run it before `apt install`.

problems.expected_output:
coreutils: /usr/bin/ls
ii coreutils
/usr/bin/tree
tree:
  Installed: 2.1.1-2ubuntu3.24.04.2
  Candidate: 2.1.1-2ubuntu3.24.04.2
problems.output_note: Version numbers depend on the Ubuntu version and the last `apt update`.
mistakes: `apt install` without `sudo`: `E: Could not open lock file /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend - open (13: Permission denied)`.
`apt install` fails with `Unable to locate package`: run `sudo apt update` first, or check the package name with `apt search`.
In Dockerfiles, `apt-get install` without `apt-get update` in the same RUN line uses old cached lists.
problems.interview_say: On Ubuntu I use `apt` to install and `dpkg -S` or `dpkg -L` to see which package owns a file. On RHEL or Amazon Linux the same tasks use `dnf` or `yum` and `rpm -qf`.
problems.try_yourself: Run `apt show tree 2>/dev/null | head -n 8`. What is the package description?

problems.title: gzip, zip, and which/type/command -v
problems.situation: The user sends a big report to a colleague who uses Windows (zip), compresses an old log on the server (gzip), and checks which program will really run when typing `python3` or `cd`.
task: Compress `report.txt` with `gzip -k` (keep the original). Compare sizes with `stat -c '%s %n'`.
Read the first line of the `.gz` file without unpacking (`zcat`).
Create `bundle.zip` from `app` with `zip -qr`. List the names with `unzip -Z1`.
Show what `cd`, `ls` and `python3` are with `type`. Show the path of `python3` with `command -v`.
hints: `gzip file` replaces the file with `file.gz`; `-k` keeps the original.
`unzip -l` lists with dates; `unzip -Z1` lists only names.
`type` knows builtins and aliases; `which` only knows files in PATH.

explanation.meaning: Compress one file into `.gz`, keep the original. `gunzip` or `gzip -d` unpacks.
Read or search a `.gz` file without unpacking it.
zip format (common on Windows): `-r` folders, `-q` quiet.
Is the name a shell builtin, an alias, a function, or a file? (`cd` is a builtin.)
Path of the program (or the name of a builtin). Best choice in scripts.
Older tool: searches only PATH files. `which -a` shows all matches.

app/

app/config/

mistakes: `gzip` on a folder: `gzip: app is a directory -- ignored`. Use `tar -czf` for folders.
Checking a tool in a script with `which tool`: on some systems `which` prints text even when nothing is found. Use `command -v tool >/dev/null`.

checks.expect: gzip: app is a directory -- ignored

problems.interview_say: gzip compresses single files and tar packs folders, so I combine them as `tar -czf`. To check which program runs, I use `type` or `command -v`; in scripts `command -v tool >/dev/null || exit 1`.
problems.try_yourself: Run `alias ll='ls -l'; type ll` in your terminal. What does `type` say now?

problems.title: Find the bug: the backup and restore test
problems.situation: `backup.sh` should make a backup of `app`, save the checksum of the backup file, and test that the backup can be restored. It prints `backup OK`, but there is no `backup.tar.gz`, and a strange file `z` appeared.
task: Run `bash backup.sh` and read every error. Run `ls`: is there a `backup.tar.gz`?
Find 4 bugs: the tar letters, the checksum target, the missing restore folder, and the false `backup OK`.
Fix the script: use `set -e`, check the checksum with `sha256sum -c`, and compare the restore with `diff -r`.
Delete the stray file `z`, run the fixed script, and print its exit code.
hints: `-cfz`: `f` takes `z` as the archive name. Write `-czf`.
`sha256sum app` fails: app is a folder. Hash the archive: `sha256sum backup.tar.gz > backup.sha256`.
`mkdir -p restore-test` before extracting. `set -e` stops the script at the first error, so `backup OK` only prints on success.
solution: [ -f z ] && echo "but there is a stray archive called z"
# Make a compressed backup of app/, save the checksum of the backup file,
# then test a restore into restore-test/ and compare it with app/.

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: with `-cfz`, the archive was named `z`, and tar tried to add a missing file `backup.tar.gz`.
Bug 2: the checksum must be of the backup file, not the folder.
Bug 3: tar -C needs an existing folder. The user sees this error only after bug 1 is fixed: now the extract fails earlier, because the archive does not exist.
Bug 4: without it, `backup OK` printed even after three errors.
A real restore test: compare every file. No output = identical.

problems.expected_output:
tar: backup.tar.gz: Cannot stat: No such file or directory
tar: Exiting with failure status due to previous errors
sha256sum: app: Is a directory
tar (child): backup.tar.gz: Cannot open: No such file or directory
tar (child): Error is not recoverable: exiting now
tar: Child returned status 2
tar: Error is not recoverable: exiting now
backup OK
there is no backup.tar.gz
but there is a stray archive called z
--- fixed ---
backup.tar.gz: OK
backup OK: restore test passed
exit code: 0
mistakes: Never testing a restore. A backup that cannot be restored is not a backup.
Keeping the checksum only next to the backup: if the disk is lost, both are lost. Store copies in another place (for example S3).

checks.expect: tar: backup.tar.gz: Cannot stat: No such file or directory
tar: restore-test: Cannot open: No such file or directory

problems.interview_say: A backup script must stop on errors (`set -e`), store a checksum of the archive, and test the restore with `tar -xzf` into a temp folder plus `diff -r`.
problems.try_yourself: Add a timestamp to the backup name: `backup-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M).tar.gz`. What else must change in the script?

problems.title: Downloads: redirects, -O and resume
problems.situation: Release download links often redirect (for example GitHub release links). The user learns to see a redirect, follow it, keep the remote file name, and resume a broken download.
task: Start the test server on port 8092 in this folder.
Request `/dist` (no slash) with `curl -sI`. Read the status and `Location` header.
Follow the redirect with `-L` and show the status code.
Download with `-O` (keep the remote name) into a new folder `dl`.
Read about resume: `curl -C - -O URL` and `wget -c URL` continue a broken download.
hints: 301 / 302 = redirect; the new address is in `Location:`.
Without `-L`, curl saves the small redirect page, not the file.
`curl -O URL` saves as the last part of the URL.

explanation.meaning: The server says: the real address is `/dist/`.
Follow redirects. `%{url_effective}` shows the final URL.
Save with the remote file name in the current folder.
Continue a partial download from where it stopped.

problems.expected_output:
HTTP/1.0 301 Moved Permanently
Location: /dist/
after -L: 200 at http://127.0.0.1:8092/dist/
todo-cli.sh
mistakes: A tiny downloaded file that is really an HTML redirect or error page. Use `-fL` and check with `file` or a checksum.
problems.interview_say: For downloads in scripts I use `curl -fsSL -o file URL`: it fails on errors and follows redirects. For big files `-C -` or `wget -c` can resume.
problems.try_yourself: Run `curl -sS -o page.html -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8092/dist` (no -L) while the server runs. What is inside page.html?

problems.title: update-alternatives: choose the default version (read only)

Change the default interactively: `sudo update-alternatives --config java`.
Check with `java -version` and `readlink -f /usr/bin/java`.
hints: `/usr/bin/java` → `/etc/alternatives/java` → the real program. Two symlinks.
`--config` shows a numbered menu; type the number and press Enter.
For an editor: `sudo update-alternatives --config editor` (nano or vim for `git commit`).

Menu to choose the default (needs sudo).
Follow all symlinks to the real file.

interview.q: How do you create and extract a .tar.gz archive?
interview.a: Create: `tar -czf app.tar.gz app/`. List: `tar -tzf app.tar.gz`. Extract: `tar -xzf app.tar.gz -C /target`.

interview.q: How do you verify that a downloaded file is not changed?
interview.a: Compare its hash with the published one: `sha256sum -c file.sha256` (or `sha256sum file` and compare). A mismatch exits with code 1.

interview.q: Which package does a file belong to?
What is the difference between `apt update` and `apt upgrade`?
interview.a: `update` refreshes the list of available packages. `upgrade` installs newer versions of installed packages.

interview.q: `which`, `type` or `command -v`: which one do you use in a script?
interview.a: `command -v tool` (POSIX, works for builtins too). `type` is good interactively; `which` only searches PATH files.
